tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`

- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always skipped for safety, even when `include_ignored` is `true`.

path.description: File or directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Omit to search the current working directory. Use Read instead when you already know a concrete file path and need its contents.

# lnav 0.14.0 — File Loading Mechanics (Area 05)

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (`lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`). All probes done by running the
binary headless (`-n`) and capturing stdout/stderr/exit codes byte-for-byte.
Scratch dir `/tmp/probe`; `$HOME` redirected to `/tmp/probe/home2` for most runs
(lnav writes state to `$HOME/.lnav`; extraction/work files go to `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work`).

Baseline test file `app.log` (169 bytes, 4 lines, LF-terminated):
```
2024-01-15 10:00:01.000 INFO starting up
2024-01-15 10:00:02.000 WARN something odd
2024-01-15 10:00:03.000 ERROR failure happened
2024-01-15 10:00:04.000 INFO all done
```
Note: this timestamp format is NOT a known log format to lnav — its debug log says
`file does not have a known text format` and `setting text format to text/plain`, yet the
leading timestamps are still recognized for time-sorting (generic timestamp detection).

---

## 1. Baseline headless behavior

- `/workspace/executable -n app.log` → stdout is the file content byte-for-byte (no ANSI
  escapes, no headers), stderr empty, exit 0.
- A file whose last line lacks a trailing newline gets one appended in output
  (`printf 'no trailing newline text' > f` → output ends `text\n`).
- `-q` suppresses the log dump entirely (stdout 0 bytes, exit 0).
- Empty file (0 bytes): exit 0, stdout 0 bytes, stderr empty.
- Any single-file open failure aborts the whole run: `lnav -n app.log /nope.log` →
  stdout EMPTY (nothing dumped), stderr error, exit 1.

## 2. Multiple files: timestamp merge & tie-breaking

- Two log files given in either argument order are merged strictly by parsed timestamp:
  arg order `(app.log other.log)` and `(other.log app.log)` produce identical, time-sorted
  output.
- Equal timestamps across files: ties are broken by file path (lexicographic), NOT by
  argument order. Args `(zzz.log aaa.log)` still print aaa.log's line first. Same result
  when both files have identical mtime.
- Cross-format merge works: a syslog-format file (`Jan 15 09:15:00 myhost sshd[123]: ...`)
  merges by time with the `2026-01-15 ...` file. Syslog lines with no year were treated as
  year 2026 (file mtime year — file was created 2026-08; current date also 2026).
- Exception (multi-member gzip, see §4): content from concatenated gzip members is NOT
  time-merged across the member boundary.

## 3. View-selection rules in headless mode (what actually gets printed)

Empirical matrix:

| Inputs | Printed |
|---|---|
| one log file | its lines |
| several log files | all, time-merged |
| one plain-text file (no timestamps) | its lines |
| two plain-text files | ONLY the last one on the command line |
| log file(s) + text file(s) (any order) | ONLY the log lines; text hidden |
| log file + `-e` exec output (timestamped) | ONLY the log file; exec output hidden |
| file args + implicit piped stdin (timestamped) | ONLY the files; stdin silently ignored |
| `-e` cmd + piped stdin | ONLY exec output; stdin ignored |
| `-` (explicit stdin) + file args | BOTH, time-merged |

I.e. headless mode prints one "top" view: the merged log view if any real log files were
loaded; otherwise a single text/exec/stdin source (the last one wins).

## 4. Compressed files

Supported, transparently decompressed, output identical to the original (verified with
`cmp`), exit 0, stderr empty:

- **gzip** (`.gz`), **bzip2** (`.bz2`), **xz** (`.xz`), **zstd** (`.zst`; tested with a
  hand-crafted valid raw-block zstd frame since no zstd CLI existed — lnav decoded it).
- Detection is by **content magic bytes, not extension**: a gzip stream in a file named
  `noext_gz` is decompressed; plain text named `fake.gz` is passed through as text with no
  error; plain text named `bad.gz` passes through.
- **Truncated gzip** (first 60 bytes of a .gz): partial decompressed content is emitted
  (ending mid-line, no newline added after the partial fragment), NO error, exit 0.
- **Multi-member gzip** (`gzip -c a > mm.gz; gzip -c b >> mm.gz`): both members decoded,
  but output is member1's lines then member2's lines — NOT time-merged across members.
- **gzip on stdin** is also detected and decompressed.
- Compressed files inside directories (arg or `-r` scan) are decompressed too.
- Extraction cache: for `.bz2`/`.xz`/`.zst` (and archives), lnav creates
  `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/archives/arc-<32hex>-<basename>/` containing the decompressed
  payload (mode `-r--------`), plus sidecar files `….done` and `….lck` (0 bytes, mode
  `-rw-------`). Plain `.gz` files did not get an `arc-` dir (streamed inline).
  The hash directory name changes when file content changes. These dirs persist after exit.

## 5. Rotated logs and `-R`

Given a base file arg, `-R` also loads sibling files matching rotation patterns.
Observed included: `svc.log.0`, `svc.log.1`, `svc.log.2`, `svc.log.2.gz`, `y.log.1.bz2`,
`y.log.2.xz`, `y.log.3.zst`, `y.log.10`, `x.log.20240114`, `x.log.old`.
Observed NOT included: `x.log-2024-01-14` (dash-date style), `ylog.1` (different base).
All loaded rotations are time-merged with the base. Without `-R`, only the named file is
loaded.

- Directory args load ALL top-level files regardless of `-R` (rotation-looking files
  included either way) — `-R` only matters for explicit file args.
- `-R` with a `.gz` base (`lnav -R app.log.gz`) FAILS: it globs `app.log.gz.*`, finds
  nothing, exit 1, stderr:
```
  error: unable to open file: /tmp/probe/app.log.gz.*
 reason: failed to find path of “/tmp/probe/app.log.gz.*”
 |        reason: No such file or directory
```
- Content-based dedup applies to rotations: when `svc.log.2.gz` held an exact copy of
  `svc.log.1`'s content, its lines were NOT duplicated in output.

## 6. Duplicate detection

- Same file twice (`lnav app.log app.log`), two copies with different names
  (`app.log appcopy.log`), plain+gzip of same content, symlink+target — all loaded ONCE.
- Debug log (`-d`) shows: `Keeping duplicated file: 9e3e94ae9b1134c0105ae4512b071a0c;
  size=169; mtime=1786218262; path=/tmp/probe/app.log` (32-hex content hash).

## 7. Directories as args

- `lnav dir` loads every non-hidden regular file directly inside (non-recursive),
  decompression included; files are time-merged.
- `lnav -r dir` recurses into subdirectories (any depth).
- Dotfiles inside a scanned directory are SKIPPED (`dir/.secret.log` not loaded), but a
  dotfile passed explicitly as an arg loads fine.
- A FIFO inside a scanned directory is silently skipped.
- A directory containing only subdirectories, without `-r`: exit 0, no output, no error.
- An EMPTY directory is a hard error (it globs `dir/*` and fails), exit 1, stderr:
```
  error: unable to open file: /tmp/probe/emptydir/*
 reason: failed to find path of “/tmp/probe/emptydir/*”
 |        reason: No such file or directory
```
- Symlink to a directory: followed, treated as a directory.
- Trailing slash on a directory is fine. Trailing slash on a FILE → exit 1:
```
  error: unable to open file: app.log/
 reason: Not a directory
```
- Glob patterns are expanded by lnav itself: quoted arg `'rot3/y.log.*'` loads all matches
  (base file itself not matched by the pattern is not loaded).
- `-r` with plain file args is harmless (files load normally).
- `--` separator works normally.

## 8. Special files

- Symlink to file: followed transparently.
- Broken symlink: exit 1, stderr:
```
  error: unable to open file: broken.log
 reason: No such file or directory
```
- FIFO as explicit arg: blocks reading until writer closes, then dumps content, exit 0
  (tested with a background writer).
- Unix domain socket as arg: exit 1, stderr:
```
  error: unable to open file: /tmp/probe/sock
 reason: failed to open required file “/tmp/probe/sock”
 |        reason: Invalid argument
```
- Unreadable file (`chmod 000`): when running as root it still reads. As user `nobody`
  (via setpriv): exit 1, stderr:
```
  error: file exists, but is not readable: /tmp/probe/appcopy.log
 reason: Permission denied
```
- Nonexistent path: exit 1, stderr:
```
  error: unable to open file: /tmp/probe/does-not-exist.log
 reason: No such file or directory
```

## 9. Standard input

- `echo ... | lnav -n` (no file args): stdin content is loaded and dumped, exit 0.
  Requires non-empty stdin: `lnav -n < /dev/null` or `printf '' | lnav -n` → exit 1:
```
  error: nothing to do
 reason: no files given or default files found
 = help: use the “-N” option to open lnav without loading any files
```
- `-N` with no files: exit 0, no output.
- Implicit stdin is IGNORED when file args are present (even timestamped stdin lines do
  not appear). Use `-` as an explicit arg to merge stdin with files (time-merged).
- `-t`: prepends the current wall-clock timestamp to each stdin line, format
  `2026-08-08T19:49:14.899295+0000 ` (ISO-8601, microseconds, `+0000`, one trailing
  space). Lines that already start with a recognized timestamp are passed through
  UNCHANGED (no double-stamping). Empty lines get stamped too (`...+0000 \n` — timestamp,
  space, nothing). `-t` has no effect on regular file args.
- Binary data on stdin → hexdump rendering (same as binary files, §13).
- gzip data on stdin → decompressed.

## 10. `-e` shell execution

- Runs via `/bin/bash -c` (error text `/bin/bash: line 1: /no/such/cmd: No such file or
  directory` for a missing command — and that text is captured as CONTENT onto lnav's
  stdout, exit still 0).
- Both stdout and stderr of the command are captured into the "exec output" view.
- The command's exit code is ignored: `-e 'exit 3'` → lnav exit 0.
- Exec output is NOT merged with log files (hidden when real files given); shown when it's
  the only source.
- With multiple `-e` flags only the LAST one's output was shown (`-e 'echo first' -e
  'echo second'` prints only `second`).
- Binary exec output → hexdump rendering.
- Each `-e` run leaves a capture file `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/piper/p-<32hex>-000`.

## 11. `-f` command file / `-c` command

- `-f cmds.lnav app.log` where the file contains `:echo hello-from-cmdsfile` → stdout is
  `hello-from-cmdsfile\n`, exit 0; the normal log dump is SUPPRESSED (echo output replaces
  it). Same for `-c ':echo hi-from-c'` (stdout exactly `hi-from-c\n`).
- `-f` with a comment-only file (`# comment only`) → normal log dump, exit 0.
- `-c ':filter-in ERROR' app.log` → dump contains only the matching line, exit 0.
- `-f` with a missing file: exit **0**, stderr exactly (note trailing spaces on line 3,
  padded to 43 chars total after the leading ` | |`):
```
  error: unknown script -- /tmp/probe/nope.lnav -- file not found
 --> command-option:1
 | |/tmp/probe/nope.lnav                   
```

## 12. Remote paths / URLs (no network performed)

- `lnav -n http://example.com/test.log` → exit **0**, stdout: `Could not resolve host:
  example.com` (DNS failure message printed as content on STDOUT, nothing on stderr).
  Same for `https://`.
- `file:///tmp/probe/app.log` works like a local file.
- `file:///nope.log` → exit **0**, stdout: `Couldn't open file /nope.log`.

## 13. Binary / invalid-UTF-8 handling

Two distinct renderings:

### a) Whole-file hexdump ("binary" files)
Triggered for heavily-invalid content (e.g. 512 bytes of /dev/urandom, truncated tar).
Exact format (from a file containing bytes 0x00..0xff):

Header line (note leading 5 spaces and trailing spaces):
```
     File Offset  00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07  08 09 0a 0b 0c 0d 0e 0f        ASCII      
```
Data rows: offset lowercase-hex right-aligned in 16 columns, two spaces, 16 hex bytes
(`%02x` lowercase, space-separated, double space between byte 7 and 8), two spaces, then a
16-glyph ASCII column. Last row is space-padded to full width. Glyph map in ASCII column
(verified for every byte value 0x00–0xff):
- `0x00` → `⋄` (U+22C4, bytes E2 8B 84)
- `0x01–0x08`, `0x0e–0x1f`, `0x7f` → `•` (U+2022, E2 80 A2)
- `0x09–0x0d` (tab, LF, VT, FF, CR) and `0x20` (space) → `_`
- `0x21–0x7e` → literal ASCII
- `0x80–0xff` → `×` (U+00D7, C3 97)

### b) Text view with per-line annotation
If the file is mostly text but its FIRST line contains invalid UTF-8 (including NUL), the
raw line is emitted VERBATIM (NUL/0xff bytes included), followed by a note and a hexdump
of just that line:
```
line one\0line two
 Line 1 at file offset 0 contains invalid UTF-8 content, the following is a hex dump of the line
 6c 69 6e 65 20 6f 6e 65  00 6c 69 6e 65 20 74 77  line_one⋄line_tw
 6f                                                o
```
(1 leading space on note/hexdump lines; same glyph map as above.) Only line 1 is
annotated — invalid bytes in later lines pass through raw with no note.

### Detection threshold (empirical, approximate)
- Valid UTF-8 control bytes (0x01–0x08 etc.) NEVER trigger binary mode, even at 50% of a
  line — only invalid-UTF-8 bytes (NUL counts as invalid here; high bytes 0x80+ that don't
  form valid UTF-8) count.
- For normal-size files the switch happens when the invalid-byte ratio is around 1/4–1/3
  of the scanned content. Data points: 48/171 file → text; 50/173 → hexdump; 980/3007 →
  hexdump; 3000/13007 (23%) → text; 64/10077 → text; 2/37 → text.
- Small single-line files are MORE sensitive: `AAA\xff\n` (5 bytes) → hexdump, but the
  same 4 bytes without trailing newline → text, and `A*7+\xff\n` (9 bytes) → text.
- Exact algorithm not fully determined (appears ratio-based over an initial sample; treat
  the above as observed boundaries, not a spec).

## 14. Line-ending and content edge cases

- CRLF: trailing `\r` is STRIPPED from each output line (`crlf-line\r\n` → `crlf-line\n`).
- Lone CR line endings (`line1\rline2\r`): `\r` is not a line separator; whole file is one
  line, interior `\r` emitted raw, trailing `\r` replaced by `\n`.
- Very long lines: 100 000-byte and 5 000 000-byte lines pass through intact (byte-exact).
- Valid UTF-8 (accents, CJK, emoji): byte-exact passthrough (`cmp` clean).
- Invalid UTF-8 bytes that don't trip binary detection: emitted raw, unchanged.
- `-S '2024-01-15 10:00:02'` prints lines with ts >= value (inclusive);
  `-U '2024-01-15 10:00:02'` prints ts <= value (inclusive). Exit 0.

## 15. Archives (.tar / .zip / .tar.gz)

- `.tar`, `.tar.gz`, `.zip` are detected by content and extracted; all member files are
  loaded and time-merged (members in subdirectories too — recursive).
- Compressed members INSIDE an archive (`.tar` containing `inner2.log.gz`) are
  decompressed recursively and merged.
- Extraction layout: `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/archives/arc-<32hex>-<archive-basename>/`
  with member files mode `-r--------`; absolute member paths have the leading `/` stripped
  (member `/tmp/x` extracts to `<arcdir>/tmp/x` and is loaded).
- **Path traversal is NOT sanitized**: member `../evil.log` was written one level up (into
  `archives/`), and `../../evil2-marker.txt` was written two levels up (into
  `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/`). Such escaped members are silently NOT loaded; exit 0, no
  error. (Would presumably write anywhere the user can write.)
- Corrupt/truncated tar (first 300 bytes): no error, exit 0 — rendered via the binary
  hexdump view.

## 16. State/work files observed

- `$HOME/.lnav` is created if missing; on first run lnav writes default config/keymap/
  theme samples and ~70 format `.json.sample` files + `.lnav` scripts under
  `formats/default/`. If it can't (fresh HOME without the dir tree), each failure prints
  `error:unable to write default config file: <path>.sample -- unable to create temporary
  file: <path>.sample.XXXXXX -- No such file or directory` to stderr (dozens of lines) and
  the run exits 1.
- `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/{archives,piper}` hold extraction/capture artifacts; they
  persist across runs.
- `-d file` writes a detailed debug log (file watch, format detection per file,
  `Keeping duplicated file: <hash>` dedup lines, etc.) — useful for a reimplementation.

## 17. Exit-code summary (headless)

- 0: normal load/dump; empty file; unreadable-by-content cases (bad gz, corrupt tar);
  `-e` command failure; http DNS failure; `-f` missing script; `-N` with nothing.
- 1: nonexistent/unreadable input file, broken symlink, socket arg, file with trailing
  slash, empty directory glob failure, `-R` on `.gz` base with no rotations, no args with
  empty stdin ("nothing to do"). On ANY input-file error, stdout is completely empty
  (loading aborts before the dump).
